EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  

================================================================  
1. Identification Strategy  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Method: Sharp regression-discontinuity design (RDD) in age-in-months around the 70-th-birthday cutoff.  

Justification  
• The coinsurance rate and monthly stop-loss cap fall mechanically for everyone on the first day of the month after turning 70; nothing else relevant (employment, pension, insurance type, provider prices) changes discontinuously.  
• Exact dates of birth, admission/visit, and discharge allow us to measure the running variable (age in months or even days) precisely.  
• Administrative universes give very large samples, so we can restrict attention to a narrow bandwidth and still retain power.  

With panel-style claims data we can additionally estimate “event-study/RD” models (difference-in-discontinuity) that compare the same individual just before and after age 70, but the core identification comes from the cross-sectional sharp RDD.  

================================================================  
2. Treatment and Control  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
• Running variable: Age in months, defined as (admission/visit/discharge/death month – birth month).  
• Cutoff: 0 at the first full calendar month in which the individual is 70.  
• Treatment indicator Di = 1{Age ≥ 0}.  
• Treated observations: Individuals observed in the first month they are eligible for Elderly Health Insurance and all months thereafter.  
• Control observations: Individuals observed just before the cutoff (e.g., ages 68–69.99 months depending on bandwidth).  

For outcomes measured only once (e.g., a death), the “observation date” is the date of the outcome; for surveys it is the interview month.  

================================================================  
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
A1. Continuity of potential outcomes at the cutoff.  
– Plausible: nothing else changes discontinuously at 70; Japan does not alter retirement age, pension eligibility, or provider prices at exactly 70.  

A2. No precise manipulation of the running variable.  
– Birth dates are fixed ex-post, and patients cannot choose when to be born. Scheduling of hospital visits could in principle respond to the policy, but that is the treatment mechanism, not a violation.  

A3. Stable unit treatment value (no spillovers across the cutoff within the chosen bandwidth).  
– An individual’s cost sharing is determined solely by her own age, and provider reimbursement is age-invariant, so spillovers are minimal.  

A4. Treatment assignment is deterministic and applied as legislated (sharp design).  
– Coinsurance rules are nationally mandated and enforced by insurers; compliance should be nearly 100 %.  

A5. Functional-form/bandwidth choice does not drive results.  
– We will show robustness to alternative bandwidths, local linear vs. higher-order polynomials, and covariate balance.  

================================================================  
4. Main Threats and Mitigation  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
T1. Differential mortality / survival bias.  
   • Older individuals inherently have higher mortality.  
   • Mitigation: Limit the sample to a symmetric bandwidth (e.g., 66–74), run covariate balance checks, and estimate “leave-out last month” (donut RD) excluding observations exactly at 70 to ensure results are not driven by deaths near the birthday.  

T2. Anticipatory behavior (patients defer expensive care until after 70).  
   • This would overstate the discontinuity in the first eligible month but is itself an effect of the policy.  
   • Mitigation: Estimate dynamic event-study coefficients for k months relative to the cutoff; look for pre-trends inside –12 to –1.  

T3. Concurrent policy reforms (fee-schedule revisions, macro trends).  
   • Any national change common to all ages is differenced out, but if another age-specific rule changes at 70 we would be confounded.  
   • Mitigation: Verify legislated rules; run placebo RDs at 68, 69, 71, 72 to show nothing special happens at other ages.  

================================================================  
5. R Code Outline (executable)  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
```r
# ------------- 0. Packages -------------
library(data.table)   # fast data handling
library(fixest)       # regressions
library(rdrobust)     # RD inference
library(ggplot2)

# ------------- 1. Load Data -------------
# Assume we work with outpatient visits from the Patient Survey
dt <- fread("patient_survey_1984_2008.csv")   # one row per visit/day

# ------------- 2. Variable Construction -------------
# Age in months at visit
dt[, age_months := (year(date_visit) - year(date_birth))*12 +
                   (month(date_visit) - month(date_birth))]

# Running variable centered at 70th birthday month
dt[, running := age_months - 70*12]           # 0 = month turning 70

# Treatment indicator
dt[, treated := as.integer(running >= 0)]

# Outcome examples
dt[, any_hospitalization := as.integer(type_visit=="inpatient")]
dt[, oop_expenses := oop_yen]                 # from claims linkage

# Keep bandwidth ±36 months for baseline
bw0 <- 36
sample <- dt[running > -bw0 & running < bw0]

# ------------- 3. Main RD Regression -------------
# Local linear with fixed bandwidth
est1 <- feols(any_hospitalization ~ treated + running,
              data = sample, cluster = ~birth_year)

summary(est1)

# Using rdrobust with optimal bandwidth
rd1 <- rdrobust(y = sample$any_hospitalization,
                x = sample$running, vce = "cluster",
                cluster = sample$birth_year)
summary(rd1)

# ------------- 4. Event-Study Visualization -------------
ev <- dt[running %between% c(-60,60),
         .(mean_visit = mean(any_hospitalization)), by = running]

ggplot(ev, aes(running, mean_visit)) +
    geom_point() + geom_line() +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, lty = 2) +
    labs(x="Months relative to 70th-birthday month",
         y="Hospitalization rate")

# ------------- 5. Robustness Check: Placebo Cutoff at 68 -------------
dt[, running68 := age_months - 68*12]
sample68 <- dt[running68 %between% c(-bw0,bw0)]
placebo <- rdrobust(sample68$any_hospitalization,
                    sample68$running68, vce = "cluster",
                    cluster = sample68$birth_year)
summary(placebo)
```

================================================================  
6. Expected Results  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Economic theory (and RAND experiment evidence) predicts that lowering the marginal price of care increases utilization. Given an approximately 60-80 % drop in coinsurance:  
• Outpatient visits: +15–25 % within the first year after age 70.  
• Inpatient admissions/LOS: smaller but positive, perhaps +5–10 %.  
• Financial risk: large fall in the upper tail; probability of monthly OOP > 20 % of income should drop by ~70 %.  
• Health outcomes: modest mortality reduction for ambulatory-care–sensitive conditions; effect size likely <2 % relative decrease in 1-year mortality.  

================================================================  
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (1 = satisfied, 0 = questionable)  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
C1. No manipulation of the running variable ............. 1  
C2. Continuity of covariates at the cutoff .............. 1  
C3. No other discontinuous policies at cutoff ........... 1  
C4. Robustness to bandwidth/functional-form ............. 1  
C5. Sufficient density of observations around cutoff .... 1  

Overall: 5 / 5 – the age-70 discontinuity in Japanese cost sharing provides a highly credible quasi-experiment.
